mainTopic: Whether public traffic cancels partitions on hard-to-use ground: רבי יוחנן on the slopes of ארץ ישראל, רחבה's challenges to רבא, and the start of the משנה on פסין for wells and cisterns.
overview: The amud opens by testing רבי יוחנן's rule, reported by רב דימי, that ארץ ישראל has no רשות הרבים. The idea that natural walls surround the land is rejected, since בבל and even the whole world are surrounded too. The real reason is the land's hills and slopes (מעלות ומורדות), which are not like the flat desert camp (דגלי מדבר). רחבה then asks רבא about a steep mound that many people walk across. According to רבנן it obviously stays private, but according to רבי יהודה it is a real question. רבא rules that one is liable, even on a slope climbed by rope. רחבה challenges him three times, with a courtyard, alleyways that open into cisterns, and the paths of בית גילגול. The first two are answered by saying their new point is about טומאה, and the third by saying יהושע gave hard paths to individuals. Finally a new משנה begins: רבי עקיבא and רבי יהודה בן בבא disagree about which wells and cisterns may use פסין.

steps.title: Rejecting the natural-walls explanation
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks whether רבי יוחנן's rule is based on ארץ ישראל being surrounded by natural walls. He rejects this, because Babylonia and even the whole world are surrounded too.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say the reason is that ארץ ישראל is surrounded by the Ladder of Tyre on one side and the slope of Gader on the other, then Babylonia is also surrounded, by the Euphrates on one side and the Tigris on the other! And the whole world is surrounded by the ocean!
steps.whatsHappening: The questioner suggests one possible reason for רבי יוחנן's rule and immediately shows that it cannot be right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steep natural formations could work as a מחיצה (partition), which would turn the enclosed area into something other than a public domain. But if that logic worked, Babylonia, which is ringed by rivers, would also have no רשות הרבים. Taken further, the ocean surrounds the whole world, so there would be no public domain anywhere, which is absurd.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (introduces a suggestion that will be rejected)
The Ladder of Tyre, a steep mountain ridge in the north of ארץ ישראל
The slope (descent) of Gader, in the south-east
Side
The ocean surrounding the world

steps.confusionAlert: This is not the real reason for רבי יוחנן's rule. The word אילימא tells you this suggestion is about to be knocked down.

phrases.english: If you say it is because it is surrounded
by the Ladder of Tyre on that side
and by the slope of Gader on that other side
then Babylonia too is surrounded
by the Euphrates on that side
and by the Tigris on this side!
And the whole world, too, is surrounded by the ocean!
phrases.notes: This takes the logic to an absurd extreme.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reasoning behind רב דימי's report (stated on the previous amud) that ארץ ישראל has no רשות הרבים.
steps.kashyaTarget: The possible reason that natural boundaries around ארץ ישראל act as partitions.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Proof by absurdity: the same reasoning would cancel רשות הרבים in Babylonia and in the entire world.

steps.title: Suggesting the real reason: hills and slopes
steps.stepSummary: The questioner proposes that רבי יוחנן meant the hills and slopes of ארץ ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps you were speaking about the ascents and descents?
steps.whatsHappening: Having rejected the first reason, the questioner now offers a better one and asks רב דימי to confirm it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new idea is about the type of ground, not about walls around it. Hilly, uneven terrain is not where large crowds travel freely. So it would not count as a public domain.

keyTerms.meaning: Perhaps
Ascents and descents (hills and slopes)

phrases.english: Perhaps you were speaking of ascents and descents?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected partition reason with a new explanation.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether רבי יוחנן's rule refers only to the hilly terrain of ארץ ישראל.

steps.title: רב דימי praises and confirms
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי tells the questioner that he understood exactly what רבי יוחנן meant.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Great mind! I saw your head between the pillars when רבי יוחנן said this teaching.
steps.whatsHappening: רב דימי answers yes. The questioner understood the ruling as well as if he had been in the study hall himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is praise, not an insult. It confirms that רבי יוחנן's rule applies to the hills and slopes, not to all of ארץ ישראל because of surrounding walls.

keyTerms.meaning: Man of the great skull, meaning a person of great mind or distinction
Between the pillars (of the study hall)
A teaching or halachic statement

steps.confusionAlert: קרקפנא sounds like a put-down, but here it is a compliment.

phrases.english: He said to him: Man of the great skull!
I saw your head between the pillars

phrases.aramaic: כִּי אֲמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן לְהָא שְׁמַעְתָּא.
phrases.english: when Rabbi Yochanan said this teaching.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 2 with a yes.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes. רבי יוחנן was speaking about מעלות ומורדות.

steps.title: Support from another report of רבי יוחנן
steps.stepSummary: A parallel report states that the hills and slopes of ארץ ישראל are not a רשות הרבים because they are not like the camp in the desert.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also stated: When רבין came, he said in the name of רבי יוחנן (and some say רבי אבהו said in the name of רבי יוחנן): For the ascents and descents in ארץ ישראל, one is not liable for רשות הרבים, because they are not like the banners of the desert.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up the conclusion of step 3 with an explicit statement of רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The laws of carrying on שבת are modeled on the משכן in the desert. A רשות הרבים must resemble the flat, open camp of the tribes, called דגלי מדבר. Slopes are not like that, so they do not qualify.

keyTerms.meaning: It was also stated (introduces a supporting source)
And some say (gives an alternate chain of transmission)
Public domain
The banners or camps of the tribes in the desert

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי יוחנן, hills and slopes are not a רשות הרבים because a public domain must be like the flat camp in the desert (דגלי מדבר).
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the rule that a public domain is defined by terrain that the public can easily cross, modeled on the desert camp.

phrases.english: It was also stated:

phrases.aramaic: כִּי אֲתָא רָבִין אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן,
phrases.english: When Ravin came, he said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ, אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: and some say Rabbi Abbahu said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan:
The ascents and descents in the Land of Israel —

phrases.aramaic: אֵין חַיָּיבִין עֲלֵיהֶן מִשּׁוּם רְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים
phrases.english: one is not liable for them as a public domain
because they are not like the banners of the desert.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the explanation confirmed in step 3.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that the slopes of ארץ ישראל are not a רשות הרבים.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבין's report (or רבי אבהו's) of רבי יוחנן's statement.

steps.title: רחבה's question about a steep mound
steps.stepSummary: רחבה asks רבא whether a mound that is steep enough to be a private domain, but that many people walk across, counts as a public domain.
steps.simpleTranslation: רחבה asked רבא: A mound that rises ten handbreadths within four cubits, and many people pass over it — is one liable for it as a רשות הרבים or not?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question. Here two rules pull against each other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Rising ten handbreadths within four cubits normally makes an area a רשות היחיד (private domain). But the public actually uses this mound as a path. The question is which factor decides: the shape of the ground or the actual heavy traffic.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked him (introduces a question or dilemma)
A mound that rises gradually
Ten handbreadths in height within four cubits of horizontal distance
Pass through it or walk across it

phrases.english: Rachava asked Rava:
A mound rising ten handbreadths within four cubits,
and many people pass over it —
is one liable for it as a public domain
or is one not liable for it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from general hills and slopes to a specific steep mound that has heavy public traffic.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether heavy public use overrides the private-domain shape of a steep mound.

steps.title: According to רבנן there is no question
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that according to the רבנן, the mound obviously stays private. This follows by קל וחומר from פסי ביראות, where the public does not cancel the partitions.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to רבנן, you should have no question. Think about it: there (the boards around a well), the public finds the area easy to use, and still רבנן say the public does not come and cancel the partition. Here (a steep mound), the public finds it hard to use. All the more so the partition is not cancelled!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins narrowing רחבה's question. It shows that according to one opinion, the רבנן, the question is not really a question at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the case of פסי ביראות, the רבנן hold that people walking through do not cancel the boards, even though that area is comfortable to walk in. A steep mound is uncomfortable to walk on, so its 'walls' are even harder to cancel. This is a קל וחומר: if the partition stands in the easy case, it surely stands in the hard case.

keyTerms.meaning: According to the opinion of the Rabbis (the majority view)
You should have no question about it
Its use is convenient or comfortable
The public comes and cancels the partition
All the more so (the conclusion of a קל וחומר)

steps.confusionAlert: The word 'there' (הָתָם) refers to the boards around wells (פסי ביראות) from earlier in the פרק. It does not refer to the hills of ארץ ישראל that were mentioned just before.

phrases.english: According to the Rabbis, you should have no question:
Now, if there, where its use is convenient —
phrases.notes: 'There' means the boards set up around a well (פסי ביראות).

phrases.english: the Rabbis say the public does not come
and cancel the partition,
here, where its use is not convenient (because of the slope) —
is it not all the more so!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows רחבה's question by removing the רבנן's view from consideration.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: According to the רבנן, the mound stays a רשות היחיד, by קל וחומר from פסי ביראות.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which opinion is the question really about?

steps.title: The real question is according to רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: The question only matters according to רבי יהודה, who holds that the public cancels the partitions of פסי ביראות. Does he agree that a steep, hard-to-use mound is different?
steps.simpleTranslation: Your question applies only according to רבי יהודה. What is the law? Maybe only there, where use is convenient, the public cancels the partition, but here, where use is inconvenient, the public does not come and cancel the partition? Or perhaps there is no difference?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now states the true form of רחבה's question. It frames the question within רבי יהודה's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה holds that a public path running through פסי ביראות cancels the partitions. The question is whether his reasoning depends on the area being comfortable to walk in. If it does, a steep mound would keep its partition status. If it does not ('לא שנא'), the public cancels the mound's natural walls too.

keyTerms.meaning: Where you should have a question
The תנא who holds that public traffic cancels partitions
Or perhaps
There is no difference

phrases.aramaic: כִּי תִּיבְּעֵי לָךְ אַלִּיבָּא דְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה.
phrases.english: Where you should have a question is according to Rabbi Yehuda.
What is the law? Is it only there, where its use is convenient (that the public cancels the partition),
but here, where its use is not convenient —
the public does not come and cancel the partition?
Or perhaps there is no difference?

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי תִּיבְּעֵי לָךְ אַלִּיבָּא דְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Having removed the רבנן's view, the גמרא states the question in רבי יהודה's view.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: According to רבי יהודה, does the public cancel a partition even where the area is hard to use?

steps.title: רבא rules that one is liable
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that one who carries there is liable. The public traffic makes the mound a רשות הרבים.
steps.simpleTranslation: He (רבא) said to him: They are liable.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives his answer to רחבה's question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Liable' means the mound is treated as a רשות הרבים, so carrying there on שבת is a real violation. The public's walking cancels the natural walls even though the slope is hard to climb. In other words, 'לא שנא': there is no difference between the easy case and the hard case.

keyTerms.meaning: They are liable (for carrying in a public domain)

phrases.english: He said to him: They are liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Public traffic cancels the mound's natural walls, so it is a רשות הרבים and one is liable.

steps.title: Even a slope climbed by rope
steps.stepSummary: רחבה asks whether this applies even to a slope so steep that people climb it with a rope. רבא says yes.
steps.simpleTranslation: And even if they climb it with a rope? He said to him: Yes.
steps.whatsHappening: רחבה tests how far רבא's ruling goes. He pushes to an extreme case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A slope that needs a rope is about as hard to use as possible. רבא still says the public traffic cancels its walls. This shows that for him, how difficult the area is to use makes no difference at all.

keyTerms.meaning: And even
They climb it by means of a rope
Yes

phrases.english: And even if they climb up it with a rope?
He said to him: Yes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the limits of רבא's answer.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the ruling apply even to a slope that must be climbed with a rope?

steps.title: Even the steep ascents of בית מרון
steps.stepSummary: רחבה pushes further, to the famously steep ascents of בית מרון. רבא again says yes.
steps.simpleTranslation: And even the ascents of בית מרון?! He said to him: Yes.
steps.whatsHappening: רחבה, surprised, tries the most extreme case. רבא holds firm.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ascents of בית מרון were famously narrow and steep. The question is asked with surprise ('?!'), as if this is hard to accept. רבא still says yes, so his rule has no exceptions based on steepness.

keyTerms.meaning: The ascents of בית מרון, an extremely steep and narrow path

phrases.english: And even the ascents of Beit Maron?!
He said to him: Yes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Pushes the limit-testing to an even more extreme case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the ruling apply even to the steepest known path?
steps.whatToRemember: רבא holds that public foot traffic cancels natural partitions no matter how hard the area is to use.

steps.title: Objection from a courtyard the public walks through
steps.stepSummary: רחבה challenges רבא from a ברייתא. A walled courtyard that the public walks straight through is still a רשות היחיד for שבת, so public traffic did not cancel its walls.
steps.simpleTranslation: He raised an objection to him: A courtyard that the public enters through this side and exits through that side is a public domain for ritual impurity, and a private domain for שבת.
steps.whatsHappening: רחבה brings a source that seems to contradict רבא's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא ruled that, according to רבי יהודה, public traffic cancels partitions even where the area is hard to use. This ברייתא says a walled courtyard, an awkward place for the public to pass through, stays a רשות היחיד for שבת even though many people walk through it. The objection only works if the ברייתא follows רבי יהודה, which רחבה sets out to show in the next steps. The courtyard counts as public only for טומאה, where doubts are judged leniently in a public area.

keyTerms.meaning: He raised an objection to him from a source
A courtyard
A public domain for questions of ritual impurity, where a doubt is ruled pure
A private domain for the laws of שבת

steps.confusionAlert: The same place can count as public for טומאה and private for שבת. Each area of law defines 'public' differently.

phrases.english: He raised an objection to him:
A courtyard that the public enters on this side
and exits on that side —
is a public domain with regard to ritual impurity,
and a private domain with regard to Shabbat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבא's ruling from steps 8–10.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's ruling that public traffic cancels partitions
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא keeps a walled courtyard, which is inconvenient to pass through, as a רשות היחיד for שבת despite public traffic. If the ברייתא follows רבי יהודה (as steps 12–13 argue), then even he holds that traffic does not cancel partitions where use is inconvenient, against רבא.

steps.title: The ברייתא cannot be following רבנן
steps.stepSummary: רחבה asks who wrote the ברייתא. If it was רבנן, the ruling would be obvious from a קל וחומר based on פסי ביראות, so there would be no reason to teach it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Who is the author of this ברייתא? If you say it is רבנן, there is a problem. Look at the boards around a well. Using that area is convenient, and still רבנן say the public does not come and cancel the partition. Here, in the courtyard, using it as a path is not convenient. So surely the partition is not cancelled! Why would anyone need to say it?
steps.whatsHappening: רחבה is trying to figure out whose opinion the courtyard ברייתא follows. He shows it cannot be רבנן, because for them the ruling would be too obvious to bother teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבנן already hold that public traffic does not cancel the walls of פסי ביראות, even though walking there is easy and convenient. A courtyard is an awkward place to walk through, so by a קל וחומר its walls should certainly stand. A ברייתא does not bother teaching something that obvious, so its author is probably not רבנן.

keyTerms.meaning: Who is it? The גמרא's way of asking whose opinion a source follows
If you say…; introduces a possibility the גמרא is about to reject
Now, if even…; opens a קל וחומר argument
Its use is convenient
The partition or wall
All the more so

steps.confusionAlert: "הָתָם" (there) means פסי ביראות, the boards set up around a well. "הָכָא" (here) means the courtyard from the ברייתא in step 11. Keep the two places straight.

phrases.english: Who is the author?
If you say it is the Rabbis,
now, if there (by the boards around a well),
where its use is convenient,
the Rabbis say:
the public does not come and cancel the partition,
phrases.notes: This is רבנן's known position on פסי ביראות.

phrases.english: then here, where its use is not convenient,
is it not all the more so!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Pins down whose opinion the ברייתא from step 11 follows.
steps.kashyaTarget: Reading the courtyard ברייתא as following רבנן
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: For רבנן the ruling follows from an obvious קל וחומר, so a ברייתא would not need to state it.

steps.title: So the ברייתא must follow רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: With רבנן ruled out, רחבה concludes the ברייתא follows רבי יהודה. That would show רבי יהודה agrees that a hard-to-use path does not cancel walls, which goes against רבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, isn't it רבי יהודה?
steps.whatsHappening: רחבה finishes his proof. The ברייתא must follow רבי יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה holds that the public cancels walls. If he still says a courtyard stays a רשות היחיד, it must be because walking through it is inconvenient. That would contradict רבא, who said in steps 8–10 that even very steep, hard paths count as a רשות הרבים.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, isn't it…? Introduces the conclusion the questioner wants to prove

phrases.english: Rather, is it not
following רבי יהודה?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion that step 12's reasoning was building toward.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי יהודה agrees a path that is inconvenient to use does not cancel walls, against רבא
steps.raayaSupportSource: The courtyard ברייתא, now assigned to רבי יהודה

steps.title: It can still be רבנן; the new point is about טומאה
steps.stepSummary: The answer is that the ברייתא really does follow רבנן. Its new teaching is not the שבת rule but that the courtyard counts as a רשות הרבים for טומאה.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Really it is רבנן. The ברייתא needed to teach that the courtyard is a רשות הרבים for טומאה.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא's side pushes back. The ברייתא can follow רבנן, because its real new point is about טומאה, not שבת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: step 12 complained that the ברייתא would add nothing according to רבנן. The answer is that it does add something. Even though the courtyard is a רשות היחיד for שבת, it counts as a רשות הרבים for טומאה. Since it can follow רבנן, it no longer proves anything about רבי יהודה, so רבא's ruling stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, actually; keeps the original reading in place
Ritual impurity
It was needed for him; it was needed to teach this
Public domain

steps.confusionAlert: The same place can be a רשות היחיד for שבת and a רשות הרבים for טומאה. The two areas of halacha define these terms differently. For טומאה, what counts is that many people pass through, because a doubt about טומאה in a רשות הרבים is ruled טהור.
steps.whyThisMatters: This answer defends רבא's ruling. The ברייתא no longer proves that רבי יהודה treats hard-to-use paths differently.

phrases.english: No; really it is the Rabbis,
and "a public domain for ritual impurity"
is what he needed to teach.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects step 12's claim that the ברייתא adds nothing for רבנן, which takes away the proof in step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Finds a different new point in the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's new point was the שבת ruling, which is obvious for רבנן, so it must follow רבי יהודה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא follows רבנן. Its new point is the טומאה ruling, so nothing is proven about רבי יהודה.

steps.title: A new proof about alleyways that open into pits and caves
steps.stepSummary: רחבה brings a new source. Alleyways that open into cisterns, ditches or caves are a רשות היחיד for שבת and a רשות הרבים for טומאה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: alleyways that open in cisterns, ditches or caves are a רשות היחיד for שבת and a רשות הרבים for טומאה.
steps.whatsHappening: רחבה starts a new attempt to prove his point, using another source. The גמרא is only quoting the source here; the argument from it comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These alleyways are hard to walk through, because they open into pits and caves, yet they stay a רשות היחיד for שבת. רחבה will try to show that this source must follow רבי יהודה. If so, even רבי יהודה would agree that an inconvenient path does not cancel walls.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear; introduces a source brought as proof
Alleyways that are open through to something
Cisterns or pits
Ditches or trenches
Caves
Private domain

phrases.english: Come and hear:
Alleyways that open
in cisterns, ditches or caves
are a private domain for שבת
and a public domain for ritual impurity.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first proof was pushed aside, רחבה brings a second source on the same question.
steps.raayaObject: That a path the public finds hard to use does not cancel walls, even for רבי יהודה
steps.raayaSupportSource: The source about alleyways that open into cisterns, ditches and caves
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's ruling that, according to רבי יהודה, public traffic cancels partitions even where the area is inconvenient to use
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Alleyways that open into cisterns are inconvenient to pass through, yet they stay a רשות היחיד for שבת. If the source follows רבי יהודה (steps 17–18), he agrees that inconvenient traffic does not cancel partitions.

steps.title: Fixing the wording: 'into cisterns,' not 'in cisterns'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the reading בבורות ('in cisterns') and corrects it to לבורות ('into cisterns'). The ruling stays the same: a רשות היחיד for שבת and a רשות הרבים for טומאה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Could you really think it says 'in cisterns'? Rather, it means alleyways that open 'into cisterns.' They are a private domain for שבת and a public domain for טומאה.
steps.whatsHappening: Before using the source from step 15, the גמרא corrects one word in it. Alleyways cannot be 'inside' cisterns, so the text must mean alleyways that lead out 'into' cisterns.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The wording בבורות makes no physical sense, since an alleyway is not located inside a pit. Changing one letter to לבורות gives the real case: an alleyway whose far end opens onto cisterns, ditches or caves, which makes it awkward for the public to walk through. The ruling itself does not change.

keyTerms.meaning: Could it enter your mind? (used to reject an impossible reading)
In cisterns (the rejected reading)
Into cisterns, opening out toward cisterns (the corrected reading)
Private domain
Public domain
Ritual impurity

phrases.english: "In cisterns" — could that enter your mind?
phrases.notes: An alleyway cannot be located inside a cistern.

phrases.english: Rather: "into cisterns"
phrases.notes: Alleyways that open out toward cisterns.

phrases.english: are a private domain for Shabbat
and a public domain for ritual impurity.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Corrects the wording of the source that רחבה brought in step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading בבורות in the cited source
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Alleyways cannot physically be inside cisterns, so that reading cannot be right.

steps.title: If רבנן wrote it, the ruling would be obvious
steps.stepSummary: רחבה asks who wrote the source. If it were רבנן, it would be obvious: they already say public traffic does not cancel the easy-to-use פסי ביראות, so it certainly does not cancel the walls of a hard-to-use alleyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: Who wrote this? If you say רבנן, then think about it. There, by the wells, where the path is convenient, they say the public does not come and cancel the walls. Here, where the path is not convenient, isn't that all the more so?
steps.whatsHappening: רחבה uses the same move he used in step 12. He shows that the ruling would be pointless if רבנן wrote it, which sets up his claim in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבנן hold that public traffic through פסי ביראות does not cancel them, even though that path is easy to use. An alleyway that ends at cisterns is hard to walk through, so by a קל וחומר its walls surely stand. A source would not bother to teach something this obvious.

keyTerms.meaning: Who is the author?
If you say
Its use is convenient (easy for the public to pass through)
They cancel (the walls)
Is it not all the more so? (a קל וחומר)
Boards set up around wells to form an enclosure

phrases.english: Who is the author?
If you say it is the Rabbis,
now, if there,
where its use is convenient,

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרִי: לָא אָתוּ רַבִּים וּמְבַטְּלִי לַהּ,
phrases.english: they say: the public does not come and cancel it,
here, where its use is not convenient,
phrases.notes: The alleyway that opens into cisterns.

phrases.english: is it not all the more so!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַנִּי? אִילֵּימָא רַבָּנַן, הַשְׁתָּא וּמָה הָתָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: With the wording fixed, רחבה tests who could be the author of the source.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that רבנן wrote the alleyway source
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A קל וחומר from פסי ביראות makes the ruling obvious for רבנן, so a source would have no reason to teach it.

steps.title: So the source must be רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: With רבנן ruled out, רחבה concludes that the source follows רבי יהודה. That would show that even רבי יהודה agrees a hard-to-use path does not cancel walls, which goes against רבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, isn't it רבי יהודה?
steps.whatsHappening: רחבה finishes his argument. If the source is not רבנן, it must be רבי יהודה, and that would be a proof against רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה usually holds that public traffic cancels walls. If he still calls this alleyway a רשות היחיד, it means that for him a hard-to-use path does not cancel walls, which contradicts רבא.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, is it not? (a pointed question that makes a claim)
The תנא who holds that public traffic cancels walls

phrases.english: Rather, is it not Rabbi Yehuda?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from step 17's rejection of רבנן.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי יהודה agrees a hard-to-use path does not cancel walls, against רבא
steps.raayaSupportSource: The source about alleyways that open into cisterns

steps.title: It is really רבנן, and the new point is טומאה
steps.stepSummary: The answer is that the source really follows רבנן. Its new teaching is not the שבת rule but that such an alleyway counts as a רשות הרבים for טומאה.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it really is רבנן. It needed to teach us that the alleyway is a public domain for טומאה.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא pushes back on רחבה's proof. He gives the same answer he gave in step 14.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The קל וחומר only shows that the שבת half is obvious. The טומאה half is not obvious: you might think a hard-to-use alleyway is not public, but because many people are found there, it counts as public for טומאה. So רבנן can be the author, and there is no proof about רבי יהודה.

keyTerms.meaning: Actually, really (keeps the original position)
It was needed for him to teach
The Sages, the majority view

steps.whatToRemember: Steps 15 to 19 repeat the cycle of steps 11 to 14. Each time, the source can be read as רבנן, because its real new point is the טומאה rule.

phrases.english: No, it is actually the Rabbis,
and "a public domain for ritual impurity"
is what it needed to teach.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects step 18's proof by finding a new teaching that fits רבנן.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Finding the חידוש (new teaching) elsewhere in the source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The source teaches the שבת rule, which would be obvious for רבנן, so it must be רבי יהודה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The source is רבנן, and its חידוש is that the alleyway is a רשות הרבים for טומאה.

steps.title: A new source: the paths of בית גילגול
steps.stepSummary: רחבה brings another source. The paths of בית גילגול, which are hard to walk on, and similar paths are a רשות היחיד for שבת and a רשות הרבים for טומאה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: the paths of בית גילגול and similar ones are a private domain for שבת and a public domain for טומאה.
steps.whatsHappening: רחבה starts a third try at proving his point with a new source. The גמרא is setting up the same analysis again with this new case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These paths are difficult to travel, yet the source says public traffic does not cancel their walls for שבת. רחבה will again want to show this follows רבי יהודה, as a challenge to רבא.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear (introduces a source as proof)
Paths of
A place whose paths were hard to travel
And similar ones

phrases.english: Come and hear:
the paths of Beit Gilgul
phrases.notes: Paths that are difficult to travel.

phrases.english: and similar ones
are a private domain for Shabbat
and a public domain for ritual impurity.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the alleyway proof is answered, רחבה brings a new source to try the same argument.
steps.raayaObject: That a hard-to-use path does not cancel walls even for רבי יהודה, against רבא
steps.raayaSupportSource: The source about the paths of בית גילגול
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's ruling that, according to רבי יהודה, public traffic cancels partitions even where the area is inconvenient to use
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The hard-to-walk paths of בית גילגול stay a רשות היחיד for שבת despite public traffic. If the source follows רבי יהודה (steps 23–24), he agrees that inconvenient traffic does not cancel partitions.

steps.title: What are the paths of בית גילגול?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a definition of the 'paths of בית גילגול' mentioned in רחבה's source.
steps.simpleTranslation: And which paths count as the paths of בית גילגול?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses to ask what exactly the 'paths of בית גילגול' are. This sets up the definition in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before arguing over who wrote the source, we need to know how hard these paths really are to use. The definition will set the level of difficulty for the whole discussion.

keyTerms.meaning: The paths of בית גילגול: steep, winding, hard-to-walk paths
And which is it? (asking for a definition)

phrases.english: And which are the paths of Beit Gilgul?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a definition of the term in the source רחבה just quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What makes a path count as one of the 'paths of בית גילגול'?

steps.title: A path too steep for a slave to run with a load
steps.stepSummary: The school of רבי ינאי defines these paths: any path where a slave cannot carry a סאה of wheat and run ahead of an officer.
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רבי ינאי says: any path on which a slave cannot pick up a סאה of wheat and run in front of an officer.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. A 'path of בית גילגול' is any path so hard that even a frightened slave cannot run on it while carrying a load.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A slave running ahead of an officer is pushing himself as hard as he can. If even he cannot manage the path with a load, the path is truly hard to use. That makes it the clearest example of an 'inconvenient' path.

keyTerms.meaning: A slave
A סאה, a measure of volume (here, a load of wheat)
An officer or soldier (from Greek)

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Yannai say:
Any path where a slave is unable
to take a se'a of wheat
and run before an officer.
phrases.notes: Even though he is afraid of the officer, the path is too steep to run on.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the definition question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A path so hard to use that a slave cannot run on it carrying a סאה of wheat, even when hurrying ahead of an officer.

steps.title: רבנן would make this ruling obvious
steps.stepSummary: רחבה asks who wrote this source. If it were רבנן, it would be obvious: they let easy-to-use פסי ביראות stand despite public traffic, so hard-to-use paths surely stand.
steps.simpleTranslation: Who wrote this source? If you say it is רבנן, there is a problem. There, by the wells, use is easy, and still רבנן say the public does not come and cancel the partition. Here use is hard, so surely the partition is not cancelled!
steps.whatsHappening: רחבה repeats the same argument he made about the alleyway. This time he applies it to the paths of בית גילגול: if רבנן wrote this source, the ruling would add nothing new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבנן already say that crowds do not cancel partitions even where walking is easy, as with פסי ביראות. So on a hard-to-use path, crowds would obviously not cancel them either. A source that says only the obvious is unlikely, so רחבה pushes the source away from רבנן.

keyTerms.meaning: Who is the author?
Its use is convenient (easy to walk through)
The partition or wall
Is it not all the more so? (a קל וחומר)

phrases.english: Who is the author? If you say the Rabbis,
now, if there,
where use is convenient, the Rabbis say:
phrases.notes: "There" means the פסי ביראות around wells.

phrases.aramaic: לָא אָתוּ רַבִּים וּמְבַטְּלִי לַהּ מְחִיצְתָּא.
phrases.english: the public does not come and cancel the partition.
here, where use is not convenient,
is it not all the more so!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies to the new source the same 'who wrote it?' argument used in step 17.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that רבנן wrote the ruling about the paths of בית גילגול.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A קל וחומר from פסי ביראות: if רבנן ignore crowds where use is easy, they certainly ignore them where use is hard. So the ruling would be pointless if it followed רבנן.

steps.title: So it must be רבי יהודה, against רבא
steps.stepSummary: With רבנן ruled out, רחבה concludes the source follows רבי יהודה. That would show even רבי יהודה agrees hard-to-use paths do not cancel walls.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, is it not רבי יהודה?
steps.whatsHappening: רחבה finishes his proof. The source must follow רבי יהודה, which would mean רבי יהודה agrees that hard paths do not cancel partitions. That goes against רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא held that, according to רבי יהודה, public traffic cancels partitions even on a hard path. If this source follows רבי יהודה and still calls these paths a רשות היחיד, רבא's view is challenged.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, is it not...? (pushes toward the only remaining option)

phrases.english: Rather, is it not Rabbi Yehuda?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion that the previous step forced.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי יהודה agrees hard-to-use paths do not cancel partitions, against רבא.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The source calling the paths of בית גילגול a רשות היחיד for שבת.

steps.title: יהושע gave hard paths to individuals
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that the paths of בית גילגול are a special case. When יהושע divided the land, he gave easy paths to the public and hard paths to private owners. So these paths are private by ownership, not because of how much traffic they get.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: You bring the paths of בית גילגול? יהושע loved ישראל. He set up roads and highways for them. Every place that was easy to use, he gave to the public. Every place that was hard to use, he gave to an individual.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא rejects the proof. These particular paths belong to private owners because יהושע assigned them that way, so they teach us nothing about public traffic in general.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רחבה's proof assumed the paths were private because people find them hard to use. רבא says they are private because the public never received them in the first place. So the case says nothing about whether crowds cancel walls, and רבא's view of רבי יהודה stands.

keyTerms.meaning: A lover of the Jewish people
Highways or main roads
He handed it over (gave ownership)

steps.whatToRemember: The paths of בית גילגול are private because יהושע gave them to individuals, not because they are hard to walk. So they cannot prove anything about רבי יהודה's view, and רבא's position survives.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רבא is saying hard paths are always a רשות היחיד. His point is that this specific case is about land ownership from יהושע's time, so it is not a general rule about traffic.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: שְׁבִילֵי בֵּית גִּילְגּוּל קָאָמְרַתְּ?
phrases.english: He said to him: You are citing the paths of Beit Gilgul?
Joshua was a lover of Israel;
he arose and established for them roads and highways;
any place where use was convenient,
he handed it over to the public;
any place where use was not convenient,
he handed it over to an individual.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: שְׁבִילֵי בֵּית גִּילְגּוּל קָאָמְרַתְּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רחבה's proof by showing that the case he cited is special.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects using the paths of בית גילגול as proof about רבי יהודה's view on public traffic.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The paths are private because of how יהושע divided ownership, not because hard use stops traffic from cancelling partitions.
steps.whyThisMatters: This ends רחבה's series of challenges. רבא's reading, that for רבי יהודה public traffic cancels partitions, holds up.

steps.title: New משנה: פסין around public and private wells
steps.stepSummary: The משנה teaches that one may set up פסין, upright boards, around a public cistern, a public well, and even a private well.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: Whether it is a public cistern, a public well, or a private well, one may make פסין around them.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It lists the water sources around which the special פסי ביראות may be set up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier we learned that פסין are allowed so travelers can draw water for their animals. Now the משנה says this applies to a cistern of collected water, a public spring well, and even a privately owned well.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה
A cistern of collected rainwater
A well of spring water
Upright boards placed around a well so it is enclosed for carrying on שבת

phrases.english: Mishna:
Whether a public cistern
or a public well or a private well,
one may make boards for them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶחָד בּוֹר הָרַבִּים וּבְאֵר הָרַבִּים וּבְאֵר הַיָּחִיד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new משנה after the previous discussion ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: פסין may be set up around a public cistern, a public well, and a private well.

steps.title: A private cistern needs a real ten-handbreadth wall
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא concludes his list. A private cistern cannot rely on corner boards. It needs a full מחיצה ten טפחים high.
steps.simpleTranslation: But for a private cistern, one must build it a partition ten handbreadths high. These are the words of רבי עקיבא.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה finishes רבי עקיבא's ruling. It names the one water source that does NOT get the easy פסין leniency: a private cistern.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The leniency of פסין is limited. A private cistern has two weak points: it belongs to one person, not the public, and it holds collected rainwater, not fresh spring water. With both weaknesses together, רבי עקיבא says the leniency does not apply, so a proper ten-טפחים wall is required.

keyTerms.meaning: A private cistern, a pit that collects rainwater and belongs to one person
A partition or wall that legally encloses an area
Ten handbreadths, the minimum height of a halachic wall
These are the words of רבי עקיבא, meaning this ruling is his view

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up בור and באר. A בור is a cistern that holds collected rainwater. A באר is a well with water that flows from a spring. The difference matters here.

phrases.english: But for a private cistern
phrases.notes: This is different from the three water sources in the step before, which do get פסין.

phrases.english: one makes for it a partition
ten handbreadths high
phrases.notes: A full wall, not just corner boards

phrases.english: these are the words of Rabbi Akiva.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבי עקיבא's ruling from step 26 by naming the exception to the פסין leniency
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי עקיבא, a private cistern cannot use פסין. It needs a real partition ten טפחים high.

steps.title: רבי יהודה בן בבא limits פסין to a public well only
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה בן בבא disagrees with רבי עקיבא. Only a public well may use פסין. All other water sources need a rope belt ten טפחים high.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה בן בבא says: One may make פסין only for a public well. For the others, one must make a belt ten handbreadths high.
steps.whatsHappening: A second תנא gives a stricter opinion. He narrows the פסין leniency to just one case: a public well.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא gave פסין to three sources: a public cistern, a public well, and a private well. רבי יהודה בן בבא allows it only when both advantages are present, meaning the source is public AND has spring water. The public cistern and the private well each have only one advantage, so they need a חגורה of ropes. This counts as a real wall because of the rule of לבוד: gaps smaller than three טפחים are treated as closed.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא who disagrees with רבי עקיבא here
A public well with spring water
And for the rest, meaning the other water sources
A belt, here a partition made of ropes strung around the area
The rule that a gap smaller than three טפחים is treated as closed

steps.whatToRemember: There are two views. רבי עקיבא allows פסין for three sources and requires a full wall only for a private cistern. רבי יהודה בן בבא allows פסין only for a public well, which is both public and has spring water. Everything else needs a ten-טפחים rope belt.
steps.whyThisMatters: The two opinions turn on how much of a leniency פסין are. Is one advantage enough (public ownership OR spring water), or are both needed? This sets up the גמרא's discussion that follows.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava says:
One does not make upright boards
except for a public well alone
phrases.notes: Public ownership and spring water together

phrases.english: and for the others, one makes a belt
phrases.notes: The others are the public cistern and the private well

phrases.english: ten handbreadths high.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a stricter, disagreeing opinion against רבי עקיבא's ruling in steps 26-27
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יהודה בן בבא, פסין are allowed only for a public well. A public cistern and a private well need a rope belt ten טפחים high.
